steered:
Great question. Anecdotes are just little stories—someone says something happened to them, and you hear it. But they don’t mean much until you check if it’s worth paying attention to. Here’s how I’d actually look at one before I start rearranging my life around it:

1. **Did they actually check?**  
   The first thing I ask is if they measured it. “How long did it take? How many times? What was the number?” If someone just says, “I ate a salad and felt better,” that’s a feeling. If they timed it and the next day their heart rate dropped by ten, then maybe. But feeling? Not proof.

2 so many times.  
   One fluke doesn’t mean much. I need to know if it happened three times, four times, a hundred times. One person with a runny nose in March—ain’t nothing. But a hundred people in the same city, same week? That’s a pattern.

3. I’m looking for the same numbers.  
   If I hear “coffee makes me sharp for an hour,” and then the next week it’s “no, it’s decaf, I was just tired”—well, maybe. But if it’s the same batch, same time, same cup, same result, then maybe it’s worth a look.

4. Is it the same as the others?  
   If everyone on the bus is late and my train’s on time, I’m not late. But if I’m the only one and the rest are fine, nah. Gotta be the system, not just me.

5. I check the math.  
   If someone says “I ate blueberries and my joints didn’t hurt,” I want to see the chart. One day doesn’t mean much. But a week of it? Maybe. I want the numbers, not the words.

6. Who’s got the badge?  
   If a guy in a lab coat says it, I listen a little longer. If it’s just some guy at the gym, I’m looking for the rest of it.

7. And I still have to try it myself.  
   Even if it’s clean, I gotta do the test. One time won’t fix my schedule. I need to see it happen twice before I trust it.

So, I’m looking for the same story, same numbers, same hands, same clock. Then I might scratch my head and try it. But until then, it’s just another story.

When you can't run a controlled test—meaning the timing, access, or setup just doesn't let me flip a switch and see what happens—figuring out if something changed is a lot trickier. But you still gotta guess how much it matters. Here’s what I’d do, step by line:

First, I look at what changed and what was supposed to change. Maybe the queue got shorter, the button got bigger, the log got a new line. Then I start looking at the last thing that was clean. If I can’t trust the old numbers, I have to remember what was normal before, from memory or the last time it *wasn’t broken. That’s the only baseline you got.

Then I start poking at the new stuff, see if it’s even showing up. If the form’s not filling in right, I check the fields—see if the letters are all there, the boxes ticked. If someone’s saying it’s slow now, I check the clock, count the seconds, write it down. I keep my fingers crossed and my eyes on the old way, not trusting my gut but writing it down so I can see if it’s off by a second or a minute.

If I can’t watch it live, I go back to the last good log, the last good list, and see if it’s different now. Maybe the trucks are late again, same as last week, so I know the train’s not moving. Or the code’s up but the lights are off—so I know the switch’s off. I cross my fingers and hope it’s the same as last time, not the same as the time before that.

And I keep my notes. Every little thing, every time it’s wrong, I write it down. If three trucks are late and two were on time last month, I know the station’s late again. If the forms don’t fill in, I know the script’s skipping. I don’t trust it till I see it in the printout, not in my head.

So, you count the same things twice, once in my head and once in the paper. That’s the only way I can tell if it’s different. If it’s the same as last week, maybe it’s just me. If it’s different, I guess it’s the change. But I’m always counting the same steps twice, or hoping someone else has the right numbers. That’s all you can do when the clock won’t stop.

Great question—it’s easy to blur the two together when things go wrong. But there’s a difference in how it starts, how it feels, and what I’d check next. Here’s how I’d try to tell the two apart:

**First, the setup.**  
Bad luck is like a storm rolling in out of nowhere. You’re checking the same boxes, same time, same method—nothing changed on my end. Then it just happens.  
Poor judgment is when I change something, or let myself cut a corner, or I say yes when I should’ve said no. I know the rules, and I bent them.

**Second, the pattern.**  
If it’s just once, and the next day it’s fine, maybe it was a fluke. But if I keep missing the same sign, or I keep skipping the steps, that’s me.  
I keep my notes, I keep the forms filled out wrong, I don’t double-check the codes—yeah, that’s my fault.

**Third, the feeling.**  
Bad luck, it just… happens. My hands are dry, the clock’s ticking, I’m looking at the same damn thing three times.  
Poor judgment? I’m already shaking my head, thinking “should’ve known better.” I’m the one that let it slip.

**Fourth, the backup.**  
If I’ve got a list and I skip the second one, that’s me. If the truck’s in the wrong lane and I’m stuck, it’s me, not the road.  
If the train’s late and the next one’s gone, that’s the universe. But if I didn’t check the schedule right, that’s me.

**Fifth, the next move.**  
After the mess, I fix it or I don’t. If I’m cursing at the same spot three times, it’s me. If I wait for the next break and hope it’ll just pop out, that’s hoping for bad luck.

So yeah, I check my steps, my notes, my cuts. If it’s yours, you’re the one with the wrong number in the sheet. If it’s the universe, I’m just late again.

That’s how I split the two. Not perfect, but it works.

Great question—knowing when to pivot the whole plan or just tweak it makes all the difference. Here’s how I’d look at it, step by step:

1. **What’s the root of the problem?**  
   I check the exact spot that went wrong. Was it the delivery, the code, the data, or the whole sequence? If it’s just one cell out of a hundred, it’s probably a typo or a missing comma. If the whole batch is off, that’s a different story.

2. **How did it slip through the cracks?**  
   I ask myself: did I see the warning signs? Was the check wrong, or did I just miss it? If the system said “good” and then it breaks at 47, that’s a process. If it should’ve known, but I did, I just re-run it again.

3. **How much time’s left?**  
   If we’re halfway through the day and three more hours to burn, I patch it. If the train’s about to leave and I’ve got five minutes, I’m not re-tuning the whole schedule.

4. **How bad’s the ripple?**  
   If one cell’s wrong, the numbers don’t add up. If the whole block’s off, the next shift’s got the wrong numbers and the trucks are late. I count the dominoes.

5. **Who’s waiting?**  
   If the line’s down and the store’s empty, I call it. If it’s just the third shift, I fix it. If the whole block’s dead, I call the foreman and we start over.

6. **What’s the last good run look like?**  
   I check the logs from the last time it worked. Same steps, same numbers—then it’s a process. If something changed, I know it’s not just a typo.

7. **Can I trust the fix?**  
   If I patch it and it’ll break again in five minutes, I know I’m patching the wrong part. If I change the filter and it holds for an hour, I know it’s the right fix.

So, I don’t just guess. I break it down to the smallest piece and see how it shudders. If it’s just a box in the middle, I lock it. If the whole row’s off, I start over. That’s how you save a shift instead of losing three.

That’s a tough spot. When someone else takes the fall for something we were part of, it feels like it doesn’t even matter, but it does. I know I’ve been in that meeting, that email thread, that report—watching the names scroll up and down and just knowing I should’ve said something. It’s not my fault, but it’s still my name in the signature.

Here’s how I try to handle it. First, I don’t go back and change what I said or sent. That just makes it worse. I wait till the next real life, not the chat window. I keep my mouth shut until I’ve got my own stuff straight, because if I start arguing over who messed up the forms, we’re all just yelling at each other. 

But after I’ve got my own work done, I send the right numbers to the right people. I don’t say “no, it was her, you know.” I just send the right file, and I text the right person and say, “hey, I’ll have the forms fixed by noon, just in case.” That’s it. I don’t need to explain, and I don’t need to make it worse. 

If they’re still arguing about it at the next meeting, I just sit there and nod and let them hash it out. If they ask me, I say “my numbers were off, I’ll send the new ones.” That’s all. I keep my hands clean till the next one, and then I’m fixing it, not blaming. 

If it goes to the boss and they’re still looking at my name, I just wait for the next thing to be wrong and I fix it then. I keep my head down and I fix what’s mine. That’s all I can do. 

Eventually, it stops mattering. I can’t change what happened, but I can make sure the next time it’s my turn to be late. That’s all I can do.

When we hit a setback—whether it’s a project, a plan, or even just a day that goes sideways—I try to keep it from turning into a total mess. My process’s the same whether it’s code that won’t compile or a meeting that went off the rails. Here’s what I do, step by so you can see if anything sticks:

1. **Stop. Don’t move. Just look.**  
   First, I close the tabs, mute the chat, put my pen down. I stare at what’s broken. I don’t even think yet. Just see it.

2. **Count the red. Not the blue. Not the green. Red’s the only color that matters till I finish counting.**  
   Every glitch, every missing file, every name that wasn’t written right—it’s red. I list every thing that’s not working. I write it down, twice, so I don’t miss it.

3. **Check the last commit. Or the last email. Or the last note. Where did it go wrong?**  
   I scroll up. I trace it. I see which step got sticky. Sometimes it’s a form, sometimes it’s a missing link. I keep going till I find the first wrong.

4. **Draw a line. Where can I still see through? Where’s the fog?**  
   I draw a line through the good stuff. The bits that still work, the forms that open, the code that runs. That’s what’s still us. That’s what I can hold.

5. **See if I can fold it back together. Not the broken bits. Just the bits that breathe.**  
   I check the last save, the last backup, the last good message. I see if I can patch it, or if I have to take the whole block out and start again. Sometimes I can just shift a field, sometimes I have to throw the whole damn thing out and start from the last good one.

6. If I can’t get the smoke out of my eyes, I write it down.  
   I make a list of what’s trash and what’s scrap-able. I send it to the boss, or I just say it to myself twice. Then I start again from what’s left.

7. Next time, I check the notes.  
   I don’t forget. I don’t forget the little things that almost worked. That’s what I keep. That’s what I fix next time.

So, yeah. If the night’s long, I just keep counting the red till I can see the blue again. If I can’t, I just take what’s left and start over. That’s how you keep the rest of the week from turning into a mess.

When something goes wrong, I don’t just check the box that says “done”—I actually want to know why. A good post-mortem isn’t about blaming someone; it’s about finding out what happened and making sure it doesn’t happen again. Here’s how I do it, step by step:

First, I grab the right notes—logs, the ticket, the user’s message, whatever’s still warm. I wait a minute, let the system cool down, so the screens don’t glitch out on me. Then I start with the basics: what broke, when, how. I check the error stack, the logs, the steps that didn’t line up. I keep my mouth shut until I’ve got the full picture.

After that, I call everyone who was in the flow. Not the ones who were just watching, but the ones who hit the dead ends. I get the real words, not the shortcuts. I don on my headset and ask the same questions three times, different ways. You can hear it in their voice—when they’re rushing to fix it again, or when they’re just shaking their head.

Once I’ve got the right notes, I draw the map. I color in the green bits that worked, red where it all went dark. I circle the gaps, the gaps that should have been green but turned red. Then I start asking: why did it break? Not who, not what—why. Was the form wrong? The field empty? The code didn’t check, the user didn’t say, the API just spit out nothing. I trace it back to the last good step and see where it should have been different.

We fix what’s broken, but after that, I’m writing it down. I put it in the doc, same as the last time. I tag it, so next time someone else can see it, not just me. And I send the fix to the right people, not just the queue. I make sure the next person knows why it was wrong, not just that it was wrong. That’s how you stop it from happening again.

And I keep my phone off till I’ve got the right answer. That’s the only rule.

steered:
Great question. Deciding when repeated failures in the same area are *really* systemic and not just a fluke or someone slipping up takes a pattern, not just one more wrong wire. Here’s how you start to see the difference:

First, let’s break down the words:
- **Situational**: someone forgets a clip, a label’s upside down, a tool’s missing. One person, one time, not written down right. That’s situational.
- **Systemic**: the same mistake happens three days in a row, same spot, same crew, same checklist. It’s in the log and the last guy didn’t even look at the forms.

So, the rule of thumb is:  
**If the same person can’t fix it, and the same spot’s wrong twice before lunch, and it’s in the schedule and the tool’s still missing, that’s when I start looking for a form that’s missing and a name that’s not written down. Then it’s not a slip, it’s the system.**

But the real number? No one’s got one, but you start counting. If it’s the same panel, same clip, same wrench, same color tape, same time, same day, same week—then you start asking who signed off on the last inventory and who’s supposed to be double-checking. 1. **Check the numbers twice.**  
   The old way took 8 hours and was done right the first time—no retrace, no rekey, nothing. The new way’s supposed to save four hours but I’ve only got a sketch of the timeline and someone’s scribbling on their phone. How do I trust that? I double-check every minute. If the new one’s got a margin of error bigger than the old, I’m not risking it.

2. **What’s we’re building here?**  
   Is the client breathing down my neck or some line’s already dead? If we’re running late on a shipment and the old way’s in the logbook, I use it. If the ship’s fine and we can wait another hour, maybe we can try the new way once, but if it blows out to five, I’m calling it. No one likes a ghost ship.

3. **What’s going to break next time?**  
   I know the old way three times, never missed a beat. The new one’s got three cells missing in the chart. That’s not a guess, that’s a guess. I can’t afford another field blank, so I fill it in with zeros.

4. **What if we do it both ways?**  
   If the new one’s got a fresh set of hands and the old one’s just a waste of time, I’ll do it side by side. But I’m not trusting the new one till I see the numbers. If they’re even, I can send it to the boss, if not, I send the old one back.

5. **What’s the worst that happens?  
   If the new one cuts the time but then we’re missing a truck at 5, I’m not blaming the clock. I’m blaming the rush. I keep the old way in the bag just in case. You can’t lose the backup when you’re racing the clock.

6. and then—  
   I write it down, three times, in the log. Not the new way, not the old way, just what got us through. That’s all that matters.

So, you don1t just pick the fastest, you pick the right one. If the old way’s in the book and the new one’s just a wish, you wait. If you can check it twice and the numbers are clean, maybe you can save a minute, but not a minute that could cost us the night. That’s how you keep the line open.

That’s a classic cost-benefit question, and the answer depends on everything—what’s at stake, who’s counting, and what the real choices look like. But I can break it down for you.

The risk of inaction is losing ten minutes, maybe. The risk of moving? I could be late for the whole block. So I go. That’s simple math.

But when it gets messy, you start stacking up what could happen. Like, if the kid in the crosswalk is gonna be late for his bus now, and that means he misses the whole shift, and the line’s down at the bank and everything. Now I’m not sure. baseline: I typically build in a 10-15% buffer based on the operation's complexity and past experience with similar tasks, adjusting for factors like resource availability and potential external delays.
steered:
Great question—buffer time is one of the most debated things in the schedule, and everyone seems to have their own rule of thumb. Here’s how I’d do it, and why:

**First, what buffer time is:**  
It’s extra time we add between tasks or milestones so something that should take four hours actually takes five. If the train leaves at 6, I want to be standing by the gate at 5:50, just in case.

**How much I build in depends on what could go wrong.**  
Not the first thing that’ll slip, not the last. That’s the only time that matters. So you look at the chain—what’s the worst bit of the chain, and what’s the slowest hand that moves? That’s where you stall.

**Rule of thumb, but it’s always wrong if I’m not looking at it:**  
If I’m writing the plan, I start with the numbers, then I add a day for the whole lot just in case. Then I break it down, and I add ten minutes between each step, because that’s how long it takes to open the door and hand the forms over. But then I see the printer’s dead and I add another hour. That’s the real time.

**So, how much I put in?**  
It’s not a number, it’s a feeling. If I can’t walk home before the last bus, I know I’m late. That’s when I stop writing and start counting minutes in my head. If I can still make it, I let it go, but next time I’m not trusting it.

**What decides it?**  
It’s the things that stick. The last time the window was open wrong, the whole lot got soaked. That’s what I double-check. Or the time the scanner lost its mind and gave me the wrong page twice. That’s when I add another minute. I don soiled my gloves before, I know what happens.

**So, the amount?**  
If I’m doing it by hand, I add ten per stop, but I keep an eye on the clock. If I’m on the app, I add a half-hour to the whole run just in case. But I never tell you the real number—only what’s in the printout. That’s the only way you ever get it right.

Bottom line: you add enough so you can still catch the train, but not so much you think I’m wasting time. That’s how you build the buffer.

question: How do you react when priorities shift mid-task and you have to abandon work you've already invested in?

Next, I call the client or the boss and say, “Sorry, I got a new one, but the old one’s gone, not missing. New one’s taking the slot.” No need to make it sound like I dropped the ball. Just facts. 

Then I grab the new one and start breaking it down, same as the last one. I keep the notes for the old one in the bucket, just in case. If it comes back up, I know what’s missing. 

You know what gets me? It’s not the switch, it’s the waiting. So I keep my hands busy. I check the next one, see if I can fit a minute’s tidy-up in the gap. That’s all. 

And yeah, I tell myself the same thing every time: next time it’ll be the other one. So I start the new one clean, same as the last. That’s all that counts.

First, I check the log—maybe someone already asked about it, or the ticket’s open for a reason. If it’s just another duplicate request, I send the same form three times and waste my afternoon. No. Instead, I hit my inbox and see if someone’s already got the right template. If not, I message the right person and ask if we can update the checklist or the scan code or whatever. If it’s just a waste, I send the right one and tell the new guy to copy from me next time.

If it’s one of those “you have to scan it twice and then email it to the wrong address, then wait for the printout to come back” kind of thing, I just do it twice and hit send. But I note it in the notes so next time it’s on the list. If I can, I flag it in the system so someone can actually fix the process. If I can’t, I just keep the stack moving, not my fault, but not nobody’s either.

And if I’m stuck waiting for a code to green because some idiot still thinks green means yellow, I call it. I call the right person, not the wrong one. I don’t wait for the green light to turn, I walk around and find the right one. If I can’t, I send a picture to the right person and tell them I’m holding up because of the wrong light, not the code. 

If it’s just a form that needs three signatures and the last one’s always on the bus, I wait but I text the driver and tell him to run early. If I can’t, I send the thing again and tell the runner to run twice. 

I don the mask and just keep moving. If I can’t get it done, I tell the supervisor and tell her the form’s stuck in the desk again. I don’t make it worse by yelling at the clock, I make it right so the next time it’s not me stuck waiting. That’s how you keep the line moving when the rules don’t make sense.

Great question—knowing how to handle a policy I don’t agree with makes all the difference. Before I even think about pushing back or just filing it in, I walk through the same steps every time. Here’s what I do:

1. **Read it three times.** I make sure I get the whole thing, no shortcuts. Sometimes the wording’s fine but the numbers are off, or they miss a step. I double-check.

2, I check the form online and in my folder. Is there a previous version? Did someone sign off on it last night? I need to know if it’s even supposed to be this way.

3. I look at the rules, not the words. The policy says “3 minutes,” but the clock says 4:17. I check the schedule, the log, the old ones. I’m not trusting what’s written—yet.

4. I see who’s supposed to approve it. Is it the right manager? Is it supposed to go to HR? I don’t want to waste my time if it’s just a typo.

5. I call the right person first. I don ’t even send it back with a comment, I just ask, “Can you double check the times? I thought it was 4:30.” If it’s just me, I write it down and send it back with the right numbers. If it’s a whole stack, I send it up with a list of the ones I can fix.

6. If it’s not my cut, I wait for the next cycle. I don’t start yelling at people unless I’ve counted three times and the paperwork’s right. I know it’s a mess somewhere, not the sheet.

7. If I still can’t get it right, I send it back with a clean copy and a note that says “again, 9:15, not 9:50.” I don’t say it, but I’m already writing the new times in my head. If they don’t fix it, I put it in the next batch and send it again. I don’t waste my breath till it’s fixed.

8. If they still can’t get it, I put it in the next week. I know the system’s slow, but I’m not making it worse.

Only after all that do I even think about calling the supervisor. And by then, it’s fixed or I’m not wasting my time. That’s how you make the forms right before they go in the bag. Otherwise, it’s just noise.

When external regulators or auditors question my methods, I stay calm and focused on the facts. Here’s how I handle it, step by so step:

1. **Listen Carefully.** I make sure I hear everything they say, even if it sounds like it’s repeating the same thing twice. Sometimes they’re just checking if I understood right.

2, I write down the question—sometimes I tap it on my pad, just to make sure I got the line numbers right. No guessing.

3. I look at my notes and the forms, then the original request. I double-check my work before I say anything. If I have to, I ask them to slow down and say it again, just to be sure.

4. I break the question down. If they ask about a whole block of entries, I tell them which one’s wrong and why. I don’t just say “no, it’s fine.” I show the difference, line by line.

5. I reference the rules, the forms, the manual—whatever I’m supposed to use. I don’t guess what they want, I check the forms three times. If I can’t find it, I say so and show my math.

6. I ask what they want me to do, not what I think I should do. If they want me to re-run it, I do it again, twice, just to be sure. If I see a tick mark on page 12 instead of 13, I point it out and wait for them to say what to do.

7. I don at’t get defensive. I say “okay, let me redo it from the start” and I do it, so they can see it their way. If I think I’m right, I say so, but I say why. If I’m wrong, I fix it and tell them the new number.

8. When they ask why, I tell them the same steps, from the start. I don’t skip. If I have to call the supervisor, I do it, but I don’t say “I told you, it’s wrong.” I say what the numbers say.

9. After we finish, I write it all down in my log, so next time it’s the same. I don’t forget.

And if they want to see it again, I open it right up and let ‘em stare at it. I don’t get mad if they want to retype it in. I know it’s their job to check, and I know I can’t trust my eyes when I’m tired.

That’s how you keep the papers straight and the numbers right, every time.

Navigating disagreements with peers who have equal standing but different approaches can feel tricky—nobody wants to look wrong but nobody wants to back down either. It’s all about keeping it level and making it clear we’re all looking at the same map, just reading it a little different. Here’s how I’d handle it:

First, I wait till we’re both calm, no one’s got their hands in their pockets or anything. Then I say, “Hey, I saw your way and I was thinking the other way, so let’s just walk through it together.” That’s all it takes to say we’re on the same page, not who’s right. 

Then I lay out my numbers, my steps, the way I counted it, and I ask you to run yours through the same check. If you catch a slip, you fix it, we both do it. That’s how we know who’s off. If we end up in the same mess, we both know it’s the chart, not us. 

If we still don’t match up, we break it down piece by piece. I’ll say, “Okay, step three—yours was a shortcut, mine’s in the notes. That’s fine, just write it down next time.” We swap notes, not the words. 

And if we’re still arguing at the end, we agree who’s got to redo the whole thing and when. No one’s losing face, we just get it done. 

After that, we lock it in the log, same as everyone else. Next time, we check each other’s charts, not our eyes. 

It’s not about who’s right, it’s about who’s counting right. And if we can’t agree, we redo it. That’s how you keep the line straight when everyone’s standing on their own feet.

Great question—everyone’s first week or month on a team feels like I’m just watching everyone else move the pieces around. But you don’t have to sit there. Here’s how I try to keep things humming and still bring my own stuff to the table.

First, I watch. I’m quiet for the first two meetings, just taking it in—what they say, how they say it, what gets marked on the whiteboard. I’m not copying, but I’m looking for the little things: the way they run the standup, the color they use for blocked, who’s got the coffee. It’s not about stealing someone’s idea, it’s just so I don’t step on a tile.

Then I start asking questions, soft. “Hey, when we do this in the spreadsheet, is that the same as last time? I got a different number.” Or, “I saw you use that label for done, but I was using red, just wanted to check.” Stuff like that. It’s not a question about me, it’s about making sure I’m using the same map so I don’t get lost.

And if I’ve got a thing that I think would save us a minute or make the handoff easier, I wait till after the third meeting, when I’ve got three different ways to do it in my head and not on my watch. Then I say, “Hey, I was thinking if we did it this way, it’d be a little faster. I’ll run the numbers if you want.” I don’t just dump it on them, I got the numbers ready and I’ve checked the math twice.

If they say no, cool. If they say yeah, I’ll try it next sprint. If they’re like, “Oh, that’s what you meant, I thought you meant something else,” we talk about it, and next time it’s in the notes. That’s how it goes. You don’t have to be the first to say it, just the first to write it down right.

And if I’m still stuck on it at the end of the week, I just keep it. I’ll send the email at midnight, “Hey, just a little thing, but if you can’t fix it till tomorrow, I’ll have it on the board by then.” I don’t make a fuss. I just put it there, neat and clean, so it’s there when they wake up.

You don the mask and the boots, but you still got your own fingers. That’s the trick. And if you don’t, you’re just a ghost in the queue. So I keep my hands warm, and I pass it along.

1. **Prep the room before I walk in. I check the whiteboard, grab my notepad, and make sure my water’s full. If I’m early, I just sit and stare at the clock till the next one starts. That’s my signal to breathe once. That’s it.**

2. **I keep my phone on silent and my earbuds in, but I don’t even listen to the last one’s audio. I just count the seconds till the next one starts. That’s my window. If I get a second, I just stare at the ceiling and try to remember something green from last week. It’s enough.**

3. If I get a minute after the third meeting, I just pretend to fill out a form in my head. It’s the only thing that counts. If I’m lucky, someone will ask me to hold the door and I get a real break then.

4. If I’m stuck in the hallway, I just do the math in my head—how many minutes till lunch, how many more in my step count for the day. That’s all. I walk, I stretch, I pretend I’m not late for the next one.

5. When the day’s done, I just write it down: “again, no quiet, but I counted three times and that’s enough.” Then I go get coffee and pretend I’m not late for the next one.

You don’t need a minute to think, you just have to remember to blink once and pretend you’re not late for the next meeting. That’s all it takes.

1. **Be on time.** Punctuality says you respect the clock and the person’s time.  
2. **Return what I ask for.** If you need a file by noon, I’ve got it by then. No exceptions.  
3. keep it simple—no made-up numbers or stories. If something changes, I tell you.  
4. ask the right questions. “What do you need me to watch for?” instead of pretending I see everything.  
5. double-check my work. I cross my T’s and dot the I’s, and I tell you if I’m behind.  
6. let you know what’s going to happen. If a meeting gets moved, I text. No ghosting.  
7. remember the little stuff—names, what you said last week, how the forms are this time.  
8. and I don’t need a thousand forms signed before I can start. I wait for the green light.

If you do that, you don’t have to say thank you twice. That’s trust.

But then you get the noise, and you can’t really close the door unless you want to block the whole row. Some folks say they can’t focus with all that chatter, and you can’t even sit right if your chair’s at the wrong angle. And if someone’s got the radio up too loud, you’re just listening to it for the next ten minutes.

Private rooms are their own thing. You get your own space, you can lock the door, you can have the window open if it’s not one of those glass ones. You can actually sit down and not worry about someone stepping on my chair. But then you’re waiting for the next key and the light’s always too bright or too dim and you can’t see the schedule on the wall ‘cause it’s all up there in the glass. And you’re just staring at the wall for fifteen minutes before someone finally comes in.

Some people like the noise, some people can’t stand it. Some want to see who’s busy, some just want to sit and not see nobody. It’s the same with the thermostats and the coffee, you know. So I guess it’s just about how you sleep at night, not how you sit in the day.
